newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen says won't compete with Deutsche Telecom.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen says won't compete with Deutsche Telecom.

text.p: Thyssen AG has no plans to compete with Deutsche Telekom in land network telecommunications, company chairman Dieter Vogel told a German freight managers congress.

The German conglomerate will maintain its stake in the E-Plus mobile telecommunications company which had built up a strong market position, he said in a speech to the annual German logistics congress in Berlin.

To gain a 10 percent share of the land network market would take an investment of 10 billion marks and initial losses of five billion marks with no clear certainty of success given that Deutsche Telecom would maintain a strong position, Vogel said.
"We will not get into this fight and will not build up our own network," he said.
Vogel said Thyssen would increase the globalisation of its core business activities, including steel making, elevators and automotive production machinery and build up its global logistics services.
Logistics could offer German companies an opportunity to reduce competitive disadvantages of high domestic costs and was a vital factor in the globalisation of production, he added.
"We must meet this challenge if we want to do something good for Germany and its competitive position," Vogel said.
Production in Brazil or Malaysia did not necessarily mean fewer jobs in Germany if the company's overall position was strengthened, he stressed.

Thyssen had reached the third stage of globalisation, with complete production of items such as ships and elevators abroad, after first exporting and then partly-producing them in other countries, he said.
The final stage would be when development centres for complete product ranges were established in selected international locations according to local costs and other factors, he said.
In its automotive division, East Asia and Latin America were gaps to be filled, while north America and Europe were already well covered, Vogel added.

Vogel said the planned Transrapid magnetic levitation train between Hamburg and Berlin, developed by a Thyssen consortium, would generate 18,000 construction jobs and 4,000 full-time posts and would be a quantum leap in passenger transport.
